video_title: Scaling Laws Roadshow at North Dakota Law: Justice Jerod Tufte on AI in the Judiciary
gist: North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte explains how he uses Claude-based AI with curated instructions and triangulated clean case data in chambers, why North Dakota treats AI as an ordinary tool without disclosure mandates, and argues that cheap AI is boosting litigation volume and access to justice while threatening courts with faster AI dispute-resolution alternatives. He pushes machine-readable law (North Dakota publishes statutes in JSON) and predicts dramatic change to the legal profession within 3-5 years.

themes.theme: Judicial AI adoption and work quality

insights.claim: North Dakota Supreme Court Justice Jerod Tufte argues judges who do not use AI likely take longer to decide cases, examine fewer potential authorities, and produce lower-quality work.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: A sitting state high-court justice framing non-adoption as a quality deficit signals growing institutional demand for legal AI tools.
insights.quote: I think the quality of your work is probably lower if you're not using these tools.

insights.claim: Tufte warns that the main risk of judicial AI use is over-trust: as tools give good results, users lose incentive to do the thinking themselves, the same complacency that sets in with a trusted staff attorney.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop verification remains the gating requirement for legal AI deployment; tools that support verification have an edge.
insights.quote: people get lazy and they they they start to want to do less work if they think they can get away with it

insights.claim: Tufte says technical knowledge of how AI models work still materially helps avoid mistakes, so he would not yet encourage every judge to dive into extensive AI use.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Legal AI adoption is still skill-gated today, which limits near-term penetration among non-technical judges.

insights.claim: Judges' main hesitations about AI are fear of embarrassing public mistakes (many face elections or retention votes), privacy and data security for sealed/confidential filings, and IT departments that have not approved tools.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Vendors that solve confidentiality, security approval and auditability will unlock the court market faster than raw capability gains.

insights.claim: Many judges are blocked from building AI workflows because court IT departments lock down computers until the bureaucracy deems tools safe for everyone.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Enterprise/government procurement and IT approval is the real bottleneck to court AI adoption.

themes.theme: Chambers workflow: instructions plus clean data

insights.claim: Tufte configures AI tools the way he would train a new law clerk, with a detailed checklist covering editing style (Red Book, Bluebook citations, Oxford comma) and workflow preferences; that instruction set combined with clean authority data is his 'secret sauce'.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Value in legal AI accrues to curated instructions and clean proprietary data, not just the base model.
insights.quote: building that instruction set, combined with good clean authority data, is then the secret sauce

insights.claim: North Dakota has no intermediate court of appeals, so its Supreme Court hears every appeal, producing repetitive criminal and family-law sufficiency-of-evidence work well suited to AI assistance.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: High-volume, repetitive appellate dockets are the first natural beachhead for judicial AI.

insights.claim: Tufte restricts his AI to a retrieval environment of published, good-authority North Dakota cases, but found Westlaw, Lexis, CourtListener and free sites each carry different patterns of publication errors, forcing him to triangulate multiple sources to build a most-reliable copy of each opinion.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Data quality in incumbent legal databases is a weakness; verified primary-source corpora are a differentiator for legal AI.
insights.quote: There are lots of publication errors in those

insights.claim: Some early North Dakota Supreme Court opinions exist only on hand-signed onion-skin paper and have not all been imaged, creating a risk of losing historical legal data.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Digitization of historical court records is an unmet need and a data-acquisition opportunity.

insights.claim: Tufte uses AI to extract every factual assertion from a brief, bench memo or draft opinion and check each against the trial record, noting briefs omit unhelpful context and that free browser tools with uploaded documents do not work well for this without proper setup.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Record-verification is a concrete, high-value legal AI use case requiring large-context, properly configured tooling rather than consumer chat apps.

themes.theme: North Dakota policy: AI as just a tool

insights.claim: North Dakota chose not to require disclosure of AI use in court filings and not to ban AI for lawyers, treating it like any other tool because whoever signs and files a document is responsible for its accuracy under existing candor and conduct rules.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Permissive state court policies lower regulatory friction for legal AI products; liability stays with the lawyer.
insights.quote: However I created this, it's mine, so I'd better check it.

insights.claim: A North Dakota court AI task force reviewed provider terms of service to identify vendors that would not train on user data and conversations; Tufte says providers have all improved on this.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Data-use and training opt-out terms are a procurement criterion for government buyers of AI.

insights.claim: Tufte warns that feeding a judge's adjudicative reasoning into AI providers risks leaks: in a high-profile case involving a publicly traded company, advance knowledge of the decision could move the stock, creating insider-trading incentives.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Court-decision information security is a market-integrity issue; trusted legal incumbents (Lexis, Westlaw) may retain an edge for sensitive judicial work.
insights.quote: that stock market could move when that decision comes out

themes.theme: Litigation volume and access to justice

insights.claim: Courts are seeing increased litigation volume as AI lets lawyers file more motions, longer expert reports, and more and lower-dollar cases in the same hours, shifting the economics of legal practice.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Rising case volumes increase court workload and demand for court-side AI tooling, and expand addressable legal markets for small claims.

insights.claim: Self-represented litigants using AI now get filings past clerk's-office formatting and certification requirements, so more cases reach judges on the merits, a burden that will fall mainly on trial courts.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Expect trial court backlogs and pressure for funding, simplified procedure, or AI triage.

insights.claim: Tufte doubts that one partner with AI bots has replaced junior associates yet, saying the industry is 'not quite there yet' even as AI acts as a force multiplier for lawyers.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Near-term law firm associate demand may erode more slowly than the hype suggests.
insights.quote: I suspect we're not quite there yet

insights.claim: North Dakota has roughly six to eight counties with no lawyers (Tufte was once the only lawyer in his county), and the host notes 17 Texas counties have a single attorney; the North Dakota Supreme Court cited AI as an access-to-justice tool in a published opinion (Helgeson) this year.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Legal deserts are a structural driver for low-cost AI legal assistance in rural states.

themes.theme: AI dispute resolution as competitor to courts

insights.claim: Tufte predicts parties will increasingly bypass courts for AI dispute-resolution alternatives, trading a slower 50/50 chance with a human judge for, say, a 30/70 chance decided tomorrow, threatening courts' relevance.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Fast AI-driven arbitration/ODR is a plausible growth market as litigants price delay as cost.
insights.quote: I feel like people will trade off the cost and the delay and go to AI alternatives to resolve their disputes.

insights.claim: Tufte argues civil procedure and evidence rules are over-engineered for small disputes and suggests a hybrid of simpler procedural channels, like small claims, combined with AI assistance applying the same law.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Procedural simplification plus AI could open new court-tech and ODR opportunities.

insights.claim: The host draws a parallel to private arbitration arising from business frustration with court delays, warning that AI judges as an alternative system could further erode court legitimacy, and argues the better answer to rising caseloads is funding more judges rather than AI detectors like Pangram or vexatious-litigant limits.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: Policy direction (funding vs. restricting filings vs. AI detection) will shape demand for court tech and AI-detection vendors.

insights.claim: Tufte says AI capabilities advance so fast that the easy way to get judges using AI is to wait six months until tools need no training; prompting skills and a custom plugin he built became largely unnecessary a few Claude versions later.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Custom prompt engineering and thin wrappers have short shelf lives; value shifts to model providers and clean data.
insights.quote: wait 6 months and the tools will be so easy to use that you won't need any training at all

insights.claim: Tufte built, in about 10 minutes, a tool that applies all of the court's rules to any PDF filing (a roughly 90% minimum viable solution), after noticing how much clerk time went to checking filings and page counts.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Court clerk compliance checking is easily automatable, signaling quick wins for court-administration AI.

insights.claim: Tufte disputes that AI tools are expensive, noting about $20 a month buys substantial access to major providers with training opt-outs and privacy protections, so cost need not create a 'trial by token' advantage.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Cheap consumer-tier models compress the advantage of big law firms' proprietary models and pressure premium legal-AI pricing.
insights.quote: I would I would disagree that these tools are expensive.

insights.claim: The host worries about 'trial by token,' where big law firms training proprietary models on decades of data, including judges' historical rulings, gain an edge, and asks whether AI parity between litigants should be guaranteed.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: Watch for AI-parity rules or norms that could affect legal AI vendors serving large firms.

insights.claim: The North Dakota legislature publishes its entire codified statutes in JSON format, with administrative regulations expected soon, and Tufte expects North Dakota to likely be the first state to provide all primary law in an AI-usable form.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Machine-readable government law lowers barriers for legal AI and erodes moats of proprietary legal databases.

insights.claim: Tufte argues the state has an obligation to publish its laws, regulations and opinions in formats accessible to AI tools, which would level the playing field for litigants using cheap models.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Open primary-law data is a structural threat to incumbent legal publishers' data advantage.

insights.claim: While checking quotations, Tufte found the state constitution text published by the legislature, and replicated by Westlaw, rendered 'Article III' as the characters I-L-L in Arial font, prompting a correction by the codifier.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Shows how AI quote-verification surfaces latent errors in authoritative legal data that incumbents propagate.

insights.claim: Pointing Claude at North Dakota's court rules to look for typos and broken cross-references surfaced over 200 errors, many from renumbered lists or publication errors, which have been incrementally corrected.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: AI-based legal code auditing is a low-hanging, repeatable service for every jurisdiction.
insights.quote: I found over 200 in our court's rules.

insights.claim: Tufte's drafting rule from the cleanup: when codifying, always add to the end of a list and avoid renumbering, since inserting items shifts cross-references to the wrong provision.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Practical drafting hygiene that reduces errors AI tools repeatedly find.

insights.claim: The host cites Stanford HAI using AI to search municipal and county codes nationwide, finding discriminatory and outdated laws that no one had time to remove.
insights.speaker: host (Kevin)
insights.so_what: AI legal-code auditing has demonstrated public-sector use cases.

insights.claim: Tufte expects the legal profession to change very dramatically in the next three to five years if models keep improving at the current rate, and says he has no advice for students starting law school now given the uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Legal services and legal education business models face significant disruption risk on a 3-5 year horizon.
insights.quote: I think our profession changes very dramatically uh in the next three to five years.

insights.claim: Tufte says AI tools are already finding tax-law loopholes that the best human tax lawyers had not found, creating arbitrage opportunities and pushing toward more flexible ways to codify and update laws.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: AI-driven tax arbitrage could prompt faster legislative/regulatory responses and changes in tax planning economics.

insights.claim: If model progress plateaus, Tufte expects a period of cleaning up archaic laws and re-engineering legal systems so AI assistants can navigate them.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Even in a slowdown scenario, demand for legal-data cleanup and system re-engineering grows.

insights.claim: Tufte argues ever-cheaper AI democratizes access to advice, from legal and financial advice to life organization and talk-therapy-style counseling, partly because people are sometimes more comfortable talking to a non-judging machine.
insights.speaker: Jerod Tufte
insights.so_what: Consumer AI advice may displace parts of professional advisory services across law, finance and counseling.
